title: Cybernetic, Allostatic, or Both? A Content Analysis of the Redox Code’s Control Architecture
content: Oxidative stress has traditionally been modeled as linear damage accumulation that antioxidants should reverse, a framing repeatedly contradicted by clinical trials. Jones’s Redox Code reframes redox state as an organized signaling system of non-equilibrium couples (NADH/NAD⁺, NADPH/NADP⁺, GSH/GSSG) and thiol switches, but does not specify its control architecture in systems-theoretic terms. We tested whether Jones’s 2024 review is better described as homeostatic (cybernetic), allostatic, or integrated — a meta-scientific question about conceptualization rather than biology. Fourteen propositions were scored against 25 pre-specified criteria across three models: allostatic (Model A, 9 criteria), cybernetic (Model B, 9 criteria), and integrated (Model C, 7 criteria). Three parallel Claude Sonnet sessions scored all 350 cells; three human raters scored a random 50-cell subset, reported as inter-rater data only. Large Language Model (LLM) reproducibility was high (Krippendorff’s α = 0.873, interval; 0.814, ordinal); human three-rater α was 0.484. LLM aggregate scores favored B (0.175 [95% CI 0.124, 0.219]) over A (0.064) and C (0.062), with a B − A gap of 0.111 [0.052, 0.164] and allostatic signal concentrated in two propositions. Applied to a standard allostatic text (McEwen and Wingfield, 2003), the same rubric returned an allostatic-dominant result (A 0.179, B 0.040). The text of Jones’s 2024 review on the redox organization of living systems is more cybernetic than allostatic, although most cells contained no control-architecture language. LLM scores were not validated against human judgment, and findings are limited to one review. The localized allostatic signal motivates a speculative three-stage control model for future testing.
